summary: EIP, the Extended Internet Protocol, is an idea paper proposing a way to grow the Internet addressing system while needing fewer changes to existing systems than other proposals, easing the transition. The author invited discussion on a mailing list. It is informational, now historic, and was replaced by RFC 6814.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine a town running out of house numbers. This paper suggests a way to add more numbers without rebuilding every street. It was only an idea to discuss, and it is now historic.

questions: what is the extended internet protocol
early proposals to extend ip addresses
subtitle: A backward-compatible way to extend the Internet's address space.

tldr.problem: The 32-bit IPv4 address space was facing exhaustion, and proposals to replace IP entirely would require massive changes across the entire Internet infrastructure.
tldr.mechanism: EIP lets routers and hosts extend addresses by adding an optional field that appears to old IP systems as a harmless unknown option, allowing gradual transition without breaking compatibility.
tldr.outcome: This RFC was an early proposal for address space expansion that did not prevail. The Internet eventually adopted IPv6 instead, which RFC 6814 superseded.

today: RFC 1385 is Historic. It was one of several proposals for addressing the IPv4 exhaustion problem in the early 1990s, and it was ultimately superseded by RFC 6814. The Internet eventually adopted IPv6, which provides vastly more addresses through a completely new protocol design rather than through backward-compatible extension.

sections.title: The Problem: Address Exhaustion and Routing Explosion
sections.content:
RFC 1385 addresses two critical scaling problems facing the Internet in 1992. First, the 32-bit IPv4 address space was being consumed rapidly; the Internet would soon run out of Class B addresses entirely. Second, routing tables were growing unsustainably because every organization needed a unique network number, and flat routing could not scale to a global Internet.

The obvious answer—replacing IP with a completely new protocol—would force nearly every system on the Internet to be modified: routers, hosts, DNS, ARP, TCP, UDP, FTP, and more. The author argues that such a wholesale replacement would be impractical and painfully slow.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet's addressing system was getting full, and fixing it by replacing everything would take forever and break everything. The paper says there's a better way.

sections.title: EIP: The Core Idea
sections.content:
The Extended Internet Protocol (EIP) separates the source and destination into two parts: a network number (which can be extended to larger values) and a host number (which stays as a 32-bit field). The clever trick is that EIP packets are designed to look like regular IP packets with an unknown option to legacy systems. The EIP ID field at position 0x8A tells EIP hosts and routers that this is an extended packet, but old IP systems simply treat it as a harmless IP option and ignore the extra data.

The EIP Extension field holds the network numbers and can be omitted for communications within the same network, maintaining full compatibility with IPv4 for local traffic. This means hosts can remain unchanged for local network communication.
sections.plainLanguage: EIP sneaks the new address information into a place that old systems will ignore, so they don't have to change at all.

sections.title: The EIP Header
sections.content:
The EIP header keeps all IPv4 fields in their original positions (Version, IHL, Type of Service, Total Length, Identification, Flags, Fragment Offset, TTL, Protocol, Checksum). Two new fields replace the source and destination IPv4 addresses: the Source Host Number and Destination Host Number, each 32 bits. After these come the EIP ID field (set to 0x8A) and the EIP Extension Length field, followed by variable-length extension data.

The maximum EIP header is 276 bytes, much longer than IPv4's 60-byte limit, allowing room for future expansion and multiple routing and addressing schemes such as Nimrod, PIP, NSAP, or even custom extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: The new header keeps the old parts so everyone recognizes it as an IP packet, then adds space at the end for the bigger address information.

sections.title: Modifications to IP Systems
sections.content:
EIP minimizes the number of systems that must be upgraded:

  • Subnet routers do not need updates during the transition, because they can treat the 32-bit Host Number as an IPv4 address and route normally.
  • Border routers must implement the EIP Extension and route on network numbers, but can provide translation service for outgoing IPv4 packets by adding the Extension field automatically.
  • Hosts must implement the EIP Extension to participate in the new system, but IPv4 hosts continue to work unchanged for local network communication.
  • ARP/RARP, ICMP, TCP/UDP checksums require no changes because they work with the host numbers as before.
  • DNS needs a new resource record type (N) for network numbers, but type A records for host numbers work unchanged.
sections.plainLanguage: Most routers don't need to change, and the ones that do only handle the new parts. Old systems just keep working like nothing happened.

sections.title: The Transition Plan
sections.content: The RFC outlines a four-phase transition. Phase 0 chooses an addressing scheme and assigns new network numbers. Phase 1 upgrades backbone and border routers and starts translation service at the border. Phase 2 gradually upgrades critical hosts like mail and DNS servers, then the rest. Phase 3 updates subnet routers and withdraws the translation service. Translation can persist as long as the 32-bit host numbers remain globally unique; once the address space is exhausted, translation ends and non-upgraded IPv4 hosts can only communicate within their own network.
sections.plainLanguage: The upgrade happens in steps, starting with the backbone routers and gradually moving to all hosts, while old hosts keep working in the meantime.

sections.title: Validation and Open Questions
sections.content: The RFC includes experimental data from 35 test hosts across 30 countries, comparing TCP throughput with and without unknown IP options. The tests showed no significant performance difference, validating the assumption that IP routers correctly ignore unknown options. However, the RFC notes ongoing debates about whether fragmentation and header checksums are necessary in a new protocol, and raises concerns about whether all Internet routers genuinely handle unknown options safely as required by the standards.
sections.plainLanguage: The author tested the idea on real networks around the world to make sure the trick actually works.
